subsubtopic: PROPOSED SUPPORT FOR THE LEGISLATED USE OF SEAT BELTS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a brief motion to read, one which I hope will find ready acceptance and which could be adopted without debate.
In view of the utterly tragic and needless toll taken by traffic accidents each year, which has spared few Canadians from the misery and grief that accompanies the inquiry or death of persons close to them, and which is responsible for the loss of over 6,700 Canadian lives a year, and in view of the singular potential held by safety belt usage for a dramatic reduction in such senseless destruction, as has been recognized by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the legislature of Nova Scotia and, now, the Government of Ontario, in their commendable actions to ensure that this potential is not lost to Canadians, I ask leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont:
That this House encourage and support the efforts of all provincial governments across Canada in implementing laws designed to protect Canadians through the legislated use of safety belts.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43 I rise on a question of pressing and urgent necessity related to the tobacco industry in Canada. Whereas the cost of production of flue-cured tobacco has increased from 1974 to 1975; and whereas the buyers of Ontario flue-cured tobacco are paying less on the auction markets than was paid at the same date last year; and whereas there is much farmer dissatisfaction with the current market prices, to the point of closing down the auction warehouses; I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise):
That this government, through the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, launch an immediate investigation into three areas of the tobacco industry. First, the buying practices and prices paid for Ontario flue-cured tobacco on the auction floors; second, the pricing of cigarettes to the Canadian consumer; and third, the possible curtailment of the export of Canadian tobacco through the pricing methods being used by the companies.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the right hon. Prime Minister following his quite correct statement yesterday that the government has limited the maximum amount of monetary benefits it can offer to the postal workers as a result of its general guideline program of controls. Has the time not arrived when parliament should be asked to intervene to restore this essential service, since the government has already restricted in fact the scope of collective bargaining on the main issue in dispute?

subtopic: POST OFFICE
subsubtopic: STRIKE OF INSIDE WORKERS-GOVERNMENT POSITION ON BACK TO WORK LEGISLATION IN VIEW OF ALLEGED LIMITATION ON COLLECTIVE BARGAINING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have had occasion before to indicate that there should not be confusion between the government's anti-inflation program, which does in fact indicate guidelines within which we hope collective bargaining will fall, and the right to collective bargaining itself. We have taken the position that employers and employees should take notice of these guidelines and find themselves bound by them in a voluntary sense. But they are only bound to negotiate in good faith. The Anti-Inflation Board will intervene if it finds that a collective agreement arrived at is not within the spirit and the letter of the guidelines.
We have interpreted the guidelines in a way which has permitted the Postmaster General to make an offer to the union. Beyond that offer it is our judgment that we cannot go without risking the offer being struck down by the Anti-Inflation Board. It is really a matter of judgment. At the present time parliament itself has certainly not indicated overwhelming or unanimous support for the position of the government, but we are letting the strike process take its normal course.

subtopic: POST OFFICE
subsubtopic: STRIKE OF INSIDE WORKERS-GOVERNMENT POSITION ON BACK TO WORK LEGISLATION IN VIEW OF ALLEGED LIMITATION ON COLLECTIVE BARGAINING
speechtext:
A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I wonder how the Prime Minister reconciles that comment with his response to the leader of the New Democratic Party yesterday, where he is reported at page 9184 of Hansard as saying:
-because of the anti-inflation guidelines we are limited in the maximum amount of monetary benefits we can offer at this time. We have gone to that limit and I think it would be misleading the people to name a mediator with that implication.
I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether it is not equally misleading to pretend that the government is not asking parliament to restore this essential service because this would interfere with the collective bargaining rights given by parliament, when in fact the government has already modified that right very substantially.

subtopic: POST OFFICE

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am afraid the Leader of the Opposition must have missed part of my answer. I answered that very question and I will repeat my answer in another form, just as the question was put in another form. I said that in our judgment this is as far as we can go as an employer within the guidelines. That remains our judgment, Mr. Speaker. It does not mean that the right of


collective bargaining is taken away. It means that this employer is trying to follow the spirit and letter of the guidelines, and has said this is as high as we can go. If we thought we could go higher there would perhaps be justification for a mediator. We do not think we can without breaking the guidelines, and if this is our thought it is our duty to make no greater offer than this because we would be subject, at least theoretically, to a fine if we went beyond what we think is as much as we can offer.

Last Friday, the office of Mr. McLish, director of civil aviation in Canada, issued a guideline stipulating that only the English language is to be used for air to ground communications in almost all cases, which revives an important debate and could have serious consequences, including disrupting the air service of the Quebec government. speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: USE OF FRENCH IN AIR TO GROUND COMMUNICATIONS- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, several Liberal members having expressed their concern to me about this matter, I have had the opportunity of examining the file. I listened closely to what the Minister of Transport had to say yesterday in the House. There seems to be misunderstanding about that matter and since emotions run high on the subject I feel that it is important that the present position of the federal government should at least be understood. The instructions alluded to by the hon. member, and about which much has been written, is not new. It is a repetition of the situation that existed, thanks to the initiative of the former Minister of Transport, and which consisted in extending bilingualism to five other airports in Quebec, under certain circumstances. Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I raised a point of order with respect to the business of the House prior to the oral question period at 2.15. Your Honour ruled that there could be no point of order raised during that period with respect to difficulties arising in connection with motions under Standing Order 43.
Unfortunately, it is not always easy to hear the preamble by Your Honour to the putting of the question, and in this instance it was difficult for me and a number of hon. friends seated around me to hear any objection to that particular motion. I know that earlier this week, on Monday, at the time of a similar circumstance, as reported in Hansard on page 9101, when a motion had actually been put Your Honour permitted the leader of the New Democratic Party to inquire, on a point of order, whether there had been unanimous acceptance of the motion.
In the same way, since it was not possible to raise the matter at the time, I would ask the opportunity tomorrow, while motions under Standing Order 43 are being considered, to put my motion, reserving the right to see whether there is unanimous acceptance.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: POSSIBILITY PRIVATE PRODUCERS ALLOWED TO COMPETE FOR GOVERNMENT CONTRACTS
speechtext:
The hon. member raises an interesting point of order. There is, of course, a fundamental difference between the two situations. In the situation in which the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) was involved a few days ago, it was the impression of the Chair that no one had withheld consent. Any hon. member, of course, was in a position to express b's resentment or unwillingness to extend unanimous consent. Further, any hon. member, even though not saying it, might have heard it from an hon. member sitting close by. It is one thing to permit a member to say that the House should take action which it can only do by unanimous consent, when it does not have unanimous consent. On the other hand, when the Chair puts a motion and hears a dissenting voice, that is the end of the matter; unanimous consent does not exist.
So this situation is quite the reverse. Although the hon. member might not have heard a dissenting voice when I asked if there was unanimous consent, I clearly heard at least one and that left me in no position to put the motion or to ask the question a second time.
The ruling I made was simply to express some concern that the revision in our procedures is such as to put a rather self-policing feature on motions under Standing Order 43. We are limited as to time, and in any case they cut into the question period. Accordingly, since they are rather self-policing in that regard, I have withdrawn


extensively from interfering with the subject matter vis-avis the words used in the rule, "an emergency matter". I did, however, express some misgivings as to whether in fact a statement by this House with regard to the use of safety belts had any urgency to it.
In any case, I resolved the doubt in favour of the hon. member, as I usually do. I put the question and I heard a dissenting voice. It would seem to me that, with slight variations or some indication that there might be a willingness to proceed with the matter tomorrow, the hon. member ought not to be in any difficulty, although perhaps he might consider whether that rule might not be as opportune an approach as, perhaps, tabling, with unanimous consent, a notice of motion by this House at the appropriate hour which would meet with unanimous approval. However, that might be something for the hon. member to consider.
While I am on my feet, there are two other outstanding points of order. The hon. member for Wellington-Grey-Dufferin-Waterloo (Mr. Beatty) raised a rather interesting objection to the treatment of a question he had placed on the order paper. I am very pleased to advise that, since the matter has now been considered, it is my understanding that there is consent in the House that since the hon. member had received a response by the government which indicated that his question would be answered some time later, under those circumstances his question ought not to have been taken off the order paper. I understand that it is now unanimously agreed that the hon. member has a good point and that the question ought to be reinstated, with the unanimous consent of the House, for an answer later.
To deal with the second point, the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) put forward a bill for first reading yesterday. The Chair, noting that the subject matter of the bill pertains to the creation of new exemptions or different treatment for exemptions from taxes, would have serious misgivings that that bill would infringe upon the financial initiatives reserved only to the Crown. In the circumstances, the only fair thing to do is to warn the hon. member now that the next time the bill comes forward for consideration, he would be expected to make some procedural justification for the bill being advanced at that time. There certainly has been some concern about that question.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE, CROWN LIABILITY ACT, IMMIGRATION ACT, PAROLE ACT JURISDICTION GIVEN TO CANADIAN COURTS TO TRY PERSONS FOR CERTAIN OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA

speechtext: The House resumed, from Tuesday, November 18, consideration of the motion of Mr. Basford that Bill C-71, to amend the Criminal Code and to make related amendments to the Crown Liability Act, the Immigration Act and the Parole Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE, CROWN LIABILITY ACT, IMMIGRATION ACT, PAROLE ACT JURISDICTION GIVEN TO CANADIAN COURTS TO TRY PERSONS FOR CERTAIN OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the conclusion of the sitting last night I had the opportunity to say a few words with respect to these amendments to the Criminal Code which the minister brought forward yesterday afternoon. I was mentioning that the action taken in this legislation to deal in particular with drinking drivers reflects a basic concern on the part of the government that we try to deal with what I referred to last evening as a growing epidemic.
The minister's move, on the part of the government, to introduce stiffer penalties is, in my estimation, both good and bad. It is good in the sense that it recognizes the problem that we are dealing with and with which we have not as yet effectively come to grips. It is bad in the sense that it may encourage people to believe that primarily through introducing this type of legislative amendment we will achieve a substantial reduction in the number of tragic accidents that take place and the number of even more tragic fatalities, or that it might also have a general impact on the number of people who believe that it is safe for them to drink to excess-by which I mean beyond one drink, or at the most two-and still get behind the wheel of a car and drive.
I have been struck in recent weeks, because of tragedies that have occurred in this country and elsewhere, with the growing concern and renewed calls for gun laws to deal with situations which from time to time lead individuals who are mentally disturbed or criminally minded to use guns as weapons of personal destruction. There is no doubt that many Canadians as well as people elsewhere are exercised by the easy availability of hand guns and other similar weapons.

Surprisingly enough, I have also come to realize that people do not share the same sentiment with respect to the number of people who believe that it is within their right, or at least that it does no great harm, to operate a motor vehicle while effectively under the influence of alcohol or some other drug. Yet to me the two situations are extremely similar in nature. They are both examples of the use, the illegitimate use if you like, of very dangerous weapons.
The fact that the automobile is not primarily thought of as a weapon is part of the mythology of our time. But if we total the hundreds of thousands of deaths which occur annually in this country as a direct or indirect result of the actions of drinking drivers, we would be shocked and I think would move to call for the most widespread and effective program that we could introduce. I realize it would not be totally within the domain of the federal government to outline such a program and put it into place, but we would certainly work quite closely, as we do with any other major problems or issues, with other levels of government, particularly the provinces.
In a recent study carried out by the Ministry of Transport on night-time driving, it was shown that one driver in four who was stopped in the course of a random hailing down of motorists driving at night was found to have been drinking. That is an indication that what we are discussing here is not a few people who are criminally minded, people we would consider to be socially irresponsible; we are dealing with what is a widespread social phenomenon, though not a problem where legal enforcement or punishment would achieve the desired result.
It is not as if we were dealing with organized crime. We are not simply dealing with a few people who will be effectively deterred by the kind of increased penalties that are set out in this legislation. As I think the minister is well aware, there are a number of well documented studies that question, in effect, the deterrent impact of legislation and whether or not it can eliminate the widespread practice of drinking and then driving.
The fact is that we have not really begun to consider what it would take to eliminate or substantially reduce the number of people who consistently drive while under the influence. I am inclined to believe the increased fines are really inconsequential. I do not think that the present fines structure accomplishes very much. It may have some deterring or economic impact upon those in the lower income levels, but it does not take into account those in the middle or upper income levels of society for whom a fine is merely a minor irritation. It may be true that the move toward an indictable offence the second time around may have some kind of general psychological, deterrent effect, but I am not overly optimistic.
I believe we are dealing with a societal and community problem of very widespread proportions. I believe these legislative amendments introduced by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) are useful only to the extent that they relate to a series of other measures which will be adopted both at the federal and the provincial level. Unless we are prepared to deal with the wider aspects of responsibility, education and rehabilitation, we will come back here three to five years after putting this legislation into effect and we will see little or no change. Indeed, even with this legislation in place, three to five years from now we might


not have noticed any substantial decrease, and perhaps a possible increase, in the number of people who are arrested and charged for these kinds of offences or, more seriously, the number of those involved in tragic accidents.
This question concerns not only the Minister of Justice, who has well defined responsibilities in his department, but other ministries of government as well. I have heard the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) express great concern at the general problem of alcoholism in our society, and perhaps he, in concert with other ministers, such as the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner), will have to give a great deal more time and attention to the way in which a concerted and comprehensive approach to the problem can be taken.
As I mentioned last evening, the province of Alberta has spent a good deal of time experimenting with a rehabilitation program. The province should be assisted and encouraged in this endeavour. Driver education and re-education programs involving the showing of films on alcohol and driving, as is the case in Alberta, and a general raising of awareness levels would be of some assistance, and it is undoubtedly true that a general alcohol education program for use in schools or by voluntary organizations should be encouraged and would fit very closely within provincial jurisdiction.
The province of Ontario as recently as last year produced a study showing that an increasing number of young drivers are involved in alcohol-related accidents. What impact does that have on the way in which young people are gradually brought into the world of driving in our society? In what way do we ensure that, through driver education programs in schools and through the actual procedure of driver training, temporary drivers' permits and actual driving examinations, there is included at every step of the way a very close relationship to the awareness of the individual of the impact that alcohol, drugs and other mind-distorting materials have on a young person's ability to operate a motor vehicle safely for himself and for others who use the highway?
We have usually regarded this kind of program as somehow peripheral and, while important in itself, not of fundamental importance in making sure that it is part and parcel of an individual's awareness as he undertakes the responsibility of driving an automobile. As I said last night, part of the problem is that things do not happen overnight. Just as we have grown accustomed to having the automobile with us-in this century we have been using the automobile as a basic means of transportation-we have grown accustomed to the epidemic proportions of those who are maimed or killed in traffic accidents.
I think it is really instructive to realize that is spite of the tens of wars that have been fought in this century, two of which we reminded ourselves about recently in our annual Remembrance Day ceremonies, and in spite of the wars that continue even to this day, there have not been as many people killed in all these conflicts as have been killed in traffic accidents in this century. When we relate this to the fact that almost every second traffic accident that occurs is the direct or indirect result of the intemperate use of alcohol or other drugs, we realize we have a
Criminal Code
problem of epidemic proportions and we know something must be done.
I mentioned the education aspect not in the narrow sense but in the very broad sense that would ensure there is an absolute awareness of the relationship between the intemperate use of alcohol and one's responsibility as an automobile driver. I think this has to work itself all the way through every aspect of the whole framework of the operation of the motor vehicle in our society.
We now have a situation in most provinces where insurance laws really act as a disincentive to the reporting of drivers who are guilty of being impaired. I wonder how much leadership the federal government has played assisting provincial governments and major insurance companies to see that there is no disincentive aspect that does not in some way or other incorporate a sense of responsibility for those who have offended the law in this way.
I have mentioned the need for education. I would also like to mention the need-this goes squarely to this bill before us this afternoon-for greater vigilance in respect of the enforcement of these provisions. It is a well known fact that there is one season of the year when the police, federal and provincial, are extremely active in the use of the breathalyzer and other forms of detection. That is, of course, during Christmas and the New Year when there are many parties and perhaps people are much more inclined to get behind the wheel of the car after attending a party when they are not sober or fit to drive.
I think that kind of selective approach is really unsatisfactory because it is obvious to me that we are dealing with a consistent pattern which is not at any one level of society, in any one part of our country, or at any one time of the year. Therefore, if we are to toughen the legislative provisions in this regard, definite action should be taken by our police forces, federal and provincial, to ensure that there is a year-round crackdown and activity in respect of ensuring that this law is enforced. In this way, people will know that if they are irresponsible enough to leave their own home or, more likely, to leave a public drinking establishment and are not capable of handling an automobile, the chances are extremely high that not only will they be stopped and questioned, but they will be arrested and charged.
I should like to make two other points which I think are important in this regard. I have said that I think the action within this legislative proposal is not in itself sufficient, though it will be of some assistance. Governments, particularly the federal government, have to consider the more fundamental question about the degree to which it has become socially acceptable to drive in this country while under the influence. I wonder how much real information we have about the types of drinking drivers that exist in this country, and how much we really know about the most effective way of getting through to them with the message that it is not right, not safe, and is simply no longer acceptable to drive while under the influence.
I think, quite frankly, we need a special task force. I mentioned to the minister last night that some months ago-I believe it was in April of this year-I produced from my own province of Prince Edward Island a report on highway safety because of our particularly shocking situation in respect of accidents and fatalities on the island. I

called the report "Half in Five". The message of the title was that if we took some definite action-and this is one of the areas we are discussing here in respect of drinking drivers-we could expect to reduce the traffic fatalities and the number of accidents by as much as 50 per cent in the next five years in the province of Prince Edward Island.
I spent a great deal of time on this report dealing with the problem of drinking drivers, because I believe it to be one of the important elements in the province. One of the conclusions I mentioned in regard to the report was that I felt the time had come to have a special task force to look into the very wide-ranging and pervasive aspects of drinking as it affects those who operate automobiles in our province and in the whole of this country.
The resources of the government of the province of Prince Edward Island are obviously limited. Perhaps they are limited everywhere in this kind of restraint. But it would seem to me to make sense, in terms of federal-provincial responsibility, if both levels of government could agree to put forward the funds for the kind of task force that could really make an examination of some of the long-term questions regarding the drug impairment that occurs and the willingness or unwillingness to accept responsibility in the operation of motor vehicles on our highways.
I have already said, and I will not repeat it, why I think that kind of a study would be important and useful. It could have a number of good recommendations resulting from it. There are a number of questions I should like to see raised, not only in analysing all the social ramifications of this large-scale phenomenon in our society but in analysing and suggesting, perhaps, some ways in which we could get at the problem.
We have never spent much time thinking about the co-responsibility or joint responsibility that exists in this regard. While we have these legislative amendments before us, it might well be worth while for the minister and his officials to consider whether the time is not rapidly coming when there must be some kind of joint responsibility exercised by those who are in an automobile and who may not be under the influence but are being driven or chauf-feured by someone who obviously is under the influence. I wonder whether that kind of co-responsibility is not a matter for some form of legal enactment.
In addition-and this is perhaps more of a hunch than a factual conclusion-since a large percentage of the people who are on the highway under the influence have left public premises, it might well be that those who operate those premises have in fact a legal responsibility. What is occurring now in my own province is that in some instances these licensed establishments, if it has been proven that people have in fact left under the influence on more occasions than is acceptable, are simply closed down and their licence is lost. This is more of a judgment matter within the particular jurisdiction of that province than any kind of general law or requirement under the Criminal Code of this country.
However, I believe it is a criminal act for people who, being aware that individuals are going to use their motor vehicles while under the influence, when they may have contributed to that situation, allow it to occur. Perhaps one

of my basic difficulties is that I am not enough of a lawyer-in fact, I am not a lawyer at all-to know hotv that would effectively be put into the law without jeopardizing any other aspects of basic individual human rights.
As long as we have the scope of tragedy, the extent of carnage that is occurring on the nation's highways in this day and age, and as long as we allow many of our fellow Canadians, young and old, to become victims, sometimes maimed and invalided for life because of those who assume they have some important right to drink and drive, we will not be acting responsibly unless we introduce the most comprehensive and effective program possible.
Therefore, I support the initiative that is taken in this instance by the minister but I would urge him and his colleagues not to leave it at that, believing that by itself this measure will be sufficient to solve this very difficult problem.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE, CROWN LIABILITY ACT, IMMIGRATION ACT, PAROLE ACT JURISDICTION GIVEN TO CANADIAN COURTS TO TRY PERSONS FOR CERTAIN OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will be very brief. Let me simply say that Bill C-71 now under consideration is a technical measure. Its only objective is to update our Criminal Code. Now what is the Criminal Code? It is the sanction of values accepted by society, the sanction of ethics and rules of conduct generally endorsed throughout Canada. It is the sanction, because those rules are accepted by the entire population. Unfortunately, certain strata of society or some individuals refuse to comply with them. Therefore, we have to draw up some regulations to force them one way or another to abide by those rules of conduct or ethics, either through the courts, the police force, the penitentiaries or prisons. Since the Criminal Code is that sanction of rules of conduct or ethics established and accepted by society, it must always be up to date and follow the changes in that total acceptance of values by society which is per se quite changeable. I thank the minister for bringing in these amendments to our Criminal Code through Bill C-71. As I say, these amendments are very technical and tend to fill some gaps that have developed in the course of years.
Indeed, one must not confuse Bill C-71 now before us, a housekeeping measure, with the long awaited amendments that will necessarily follow the findings of the Law Reform Commission which, in recent months, has supplied us with all kinds of work documents and studies on the various aspects it has considered, particularly family law, evidence, sentencing, judicialization, all law matters that have to be reformed in depth. We are waiting for the results of these works with great impatience and I hope we will see them soon embodied in a bill introduced in this House.
Therefore these technical amendments cover aspects of the Criminal Code in almost every reach in sections of current application, be it theft, rape, internationally protected persons or still, more technically, in the field of procedure. In the procedural area, for instance, this bill proposes a number of improvements which law practitioners had been requesting for quite some time. These include Clause 94, page 60, to amend the section on the trial de novo system in summary conviction matters so that, when the


amount is somewhat minimal and when an appeal has been filed, there must be a new trial.
Therefore these provisions on de novo trials will be amended so that courts of higher instance may assess more easily the evidence introduced before a court of first instance, without the appellant having to establish again this evidence. In this respect, I share somewhat the fears which the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) expressed when he said that giving such a power of assessment to courts of appeal could cause problems in terms of court accessibility. I feel however that this difficulty could be examined in committee, as most of the clauses in Bill C-71 for that matter, for it is in committee that they should be examined in detail one after the other.
Since we must discuss the bill's general principle on second reading, I will concern myself with a question perhaps a little more important, that is one of the two or three items dealt with by Bill C-71 which may be of major importance and show, like a lighthouse would do for a deep water harbour or still water zone, what the global reform of criminal law will be like in Canada.
I want especially to discuss the amendments relating to evidence with regard to rape cases. I also want to discuss the protection granted to individuals having diplomatic or international status. I feel there is a gap in this area in Canads which Bill C-71 is trying to fill. There again we will review in committee the consequences of those new sections of the law.
What I want to discuss more fully is the provision about the corroboration and the amendments to the principle of evidence in cases of rape or other sexual offences, amendments brought in by Bill C-71.
Corroboration is a somewhat strange legal phenomenon. In fact, this stratagem of proof, if I can use such terms, was originally introduced in common law to support the evidence of witnesses whose credibility was questionable in the minds of the jurists of that time. We know that in common law and in criminal law, especially in Canada, one proof is enough to convict a person. The one proof is sufficient, precisely to the extent that the credibility of the witness can be estimated.
Now, for instance, in the case of rape, the jury can convict somebody of rape on the strength of the victim's evidence alone. But rightly or wrongly, it has been considered for a very long time, in sexual offences, that because of the emotional aspect involved, the credibility of the witness was questionable to say the least. I want to point out here that, probably more wrongly than rightly, the judge was requested, when making his address to the jury, to make sure he pointed out the dangers of condemning the accused merely on the strength of the victim's testimony. And so, what is corroboration? It is the possibility for the jury of weighing a second proof, a secondary testimony, secondary in the sense that it must not necessarily be related to the main proof. What does that mean? That if, for instance, there is an element of proof with regard to the victim, another element of proof, which differs from the other but is related in a way, of course, to the main accusation, then, there is corroboration and it will be easier for the jury to pass judgment on the guilt or innocence of the accused.
Criminal Code
Therefore corroboration was a type of judicial animal developed specially for particular cases such as sexual crimes, or for cases where children appeared as witnesses, where they are unable to swear to their testimony, or again in the case of perjury, treason, false evidence and finally the testimony of accomplices.
They are quite particular cases where corroboration is necessary, cases where the credibility of the main witness may be very doubtful. Then, we can again ask ourselves if in cases of rape or sexual offences we should demand corroboration. I think that some historical considerations are necessary and that we must realize that 200 or 300 years ago the status of women was not the same as today. The status of women has much improved to become in 1975 equal to that of man.
But 300 years ago the circumstances were different and women perhaps considered as merchandise. What was rape at the origin? It was the fact of taking a woman without the consent of her legal owner, her husband, her father or someone else. The principle of corroboration may stem from that because at the time women were unimportant and it was then necessary to produce more evidence than in normal cases in order to condemn those who made an attempt against that property.
We realize that this concept now belongs to the past particularly in this womens' year that gives official recognition to that principle of equal status on which we all agree. So that whole concept of corroboration and sexual conduct in cases concerning women should be changed and the elimination of corroboration, or rather the address to the jury, is a positive step in this direction.
It is not enough. I think we should come to a more comprehensive and less sectarian definition of sexual offences and stop making reference to sexual offences involving female persons, and try instead to clarify this concept of sexual offence so that it is embodied in the whole section of Criminal Code concerning assaults. It could be an ordinary assault, an assault causing injury, a serious assault, a less serious assault, in short a sexual offence is generally an assault in the broad meaning of the term. I for one would favour the incorporation of offences of a sexual nature into offences of the "assault" type; we should stop considering sexual offences as a little sordid. They are sometimes sordid, but not always.
It is often said that 60 per cent of the cases of rape happen between people who know each other intimately. Therefore I think the scandalous nature should be removed from sexual offences. We must stop referring to sexual offences as being mainly related to female persons. We should include all these types of offences-rape, indecent assault, sexual assault on people who are less than 14 years old-in the sections on assault which are complete, precise, by adding one definition or two to the general nature of assaults; it will be possible to include these offences in sections on assault, thereby removing a little of this scandalous context from the Criminal Code.
So Bill C-71 aims at correcting what had almost become the victim's trial in cases of rape by removing the address to the jury in respect of corroboration, and I think it is a very important step forward. Once again, I agree a little
9248


Criminal Code
however with the reservations made yesterday by the hon. member for Calgary-North (Mr. Woolliams). I appreciated them very much. His very wide legal experience will no doubt be of great help in committee when we study in depth the clauses of Bill C-71. I shared his reservations when he wondered whether henceforth the credibility of the witness could really not be questioned if all emotivity surrounding sexual crimes was truly abolished, and if evidence by the victim alone was really sufficient in rape cases for the jury to render a guilty or non guilty verdict in every case.
I submit, Madam Speaker, as is documented by psychological, empirical and other studies, that the jury is somewhat less stupid than commonly imagined, and that jurors are much more alert and educated now. They can judge by themselves, without the need for an extra witness and for someone to show them the road to follow. They can now judge by themselves the credibility of the witness about to speak before them, and the greater or lesser weight of his evidence.
The jury as an institution and its importance have been been discussed at length. In my view, the jury may be the most remarkable institution in our criminal law, in that twelve people that may not have a solid legal background are asked to examine, in their conscience, the facts that are presented. The jury must therefore rely on facts, and weigh them according to their merit. They must also assess the witness's credibility. I feel they are fully capable to do so without the need of concepts as archaic as corroboration, especially in cases of criminal offences.
In my view, the final solution to all offences in that nature would be, in order to strip them of any obscene aspect they now have, to include them altogether with the sections on assault. This will solve a number of problems concerning evidence, appreciation, publicity and credibility, and all the evidence problems that have developed and that arise in this kind of court proceedings.
Madam Speaker, I said I would be brief, I believe this is a housekeeping kind of bill, to update the Criminal Code. I do not think there is much to say in substance, except that it was necessary precisely to enable legal practitioners to use the Criminal Code in a sensible way. We are all looking forward to the implementation of the comprehensive reform of the Criminal Code following the studies of the Law Reform Commission. We hope that this in depth- really in depth-reform will enable us to do away with all the dead-weight that has accumulated for centuries in the Criminal Code. We hope a thorough study will be carried out to define the goals we aimed at with the Criminal Code, and insofar as the whole matter of crime and fight against crime through a criminal code will be questioned, I shall be satisfied. Until then, I only hope that Bill C-71 will be passed shortly, for legal practitioners badly need it.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I go back to this very specific example. Police officers, on behalf of all, governments and society, will attempt to preserve not only the citizens' life but also their property. They have to make a choice, and that choice is made on our behalf, in the name of society and that of this country's authority, namely to do everything to protect themselves and protect the citizens' life.
If gangsters use weapons, police officers must also use them to defend society and property. This is where the whole tragedy occurs; we are talking about it today and the Law Reform Commission, does the same and we will talk about it again if the minister honours his promise to proceed with an in depth reform of the Criminal Code.
When our law enforcement authorities obtain equipment which is at least equivalent to that which is available to gangster chiefs, forces are matched; laws must be applied on the basis of our trust in our police forces.
Well, it is the opposite which happens now in our society, for policemen are doing their jobs, risking their lives arresting gangsters, and often losing their lives or their limbs in the process, as was recently the case in Victoria-ville, Drummondville, Moncton and several other communities. Later on, gangsters are put in jail where they live in comfortable cells, judgments in their case are quickly rendered and, not long after that, we hear that they are out again and that they have committed other crimes. Who decided that they should be released and why? Very often, some of them are even paroled by mistake. Such was the case recently in Montreal. They have to run after the prisoner. Madam Speaker, the morale of our law enforcement authorities has never been so low. Even if we adopted the most beautiful gold-lettered Criminal Code unanimously endorsed by this House, if in daily practice we were not able to give our enforcement authorities the necessary confidence and the assurance that they are backed up by the legislative authorities, we would have wasted our time. This is true whether we want to maintain law and order or administer this legislation.


Criminal Code
Somewhere in this bill, there is a provision on road-side screening devices. It is the same thing. This is enforced every day. That is what is meant by protection of society. Many people would like to go through red lights and stop at green lights. That is what I would like anyway. But the law is not made that way, Madam Speaker. We have to abide by it. There must be some order in society. We really must have the mind and the will to enforce it.
That is why I cannot believe in the seriousness and goodwill of the government when it agrees that the Minister should put his head on the block on the matter of capital punishment, when we already have a legislation which is not enforced or which the cabinet refuses to enforce.
Madam Speaker, that is why I am very sceptical about the mini-reform which Bill C-71 constitutes; finally, it is nothing but a very superficial rewrite.
I would describe it as window dressing. It will allow some policemen to say that the federal Parliament takes care of order in society, but it will change nothing in the rising crime index in Canada, the failure of the rehabilata-tion program in the last four or five years. Nor will it change anything in the speed with which justice is done today. We need but look at the number of people who wait for months and months before appearing in court; nor will it change anything in the type of scandal we read about in the newspapers, and which are brought to light thanks to the extraordinary work of the Quebec Police Commission probe into organized crime. Full pages of it are published; yet, we had a Criminal Code. I remember how, in 1968, we studied the omnibus bill which dealt with all manners of subjects.
I remember the then Minister of Justice saying how wonderful the bill was, that it was a new approach. It was fantastic, it would allow the tracking down of gangsters to come, thanks to the use of electronic wire-tapping devices. Well, this is more of the same. It demonstrates once again that our approach is erroneous, that we are not really sincere in the fight against crime, that we are not really efficient in the rehabilitation of criminals.
Madam Speaker, I would like to reserve my remarks on this subject. Since it bears on general points, I shall certainly follow this bill closely and, unlike the minister, I am not overly anxious to approve a bill which, ultimately has virtually no meaning. It would be important to tell the minister that his endeavour, his patience in listening to us are basically a waste of time since this bill changes absolutely nothing but words; it contains no in-depth change.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, may I first of all identify myself with some of the remarks made by the hon. member who immediately preceded me in this debate, the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin). I think it is just as germane, with all respect to the interven-or, to discuss what is not in a bill as it is to discuss what is in a bill; that is, to discuss, particularly on second reading, what is contained therein.
I listened with considerable interest to the hon. member for Lafontaine-Rosemont (Mr. Lachance) and I agree with

what he said. He said that this bill is an updating of the Criminal Code, a housekeeping measure, simply another in the series of patchwork measures to amend the Criminal Code. Those who have been victims of the old Criminal Code, or those of us who act as counsel, may have other views. I am delighted to see the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Blais) here; I am sure he is familiar with the legislation.
For many generations we have been living with a code that has been, because of public pressure or otherwise, or government leadership, subject to updating from time to time. I do not want the minister or anyone else to misunderstand my remarks. This is absolutely necessary in any moral legislation. But those of us who agree with what was said by the hon. member for Lotbiniere feel that perhaps the time has come to approach the code in a different way and take a broader view.
I do not want to prolong this debate and I intend to confine my remarks to that part of the bill related to sexual offences. I should like to deal with some of the others becaue they concern all of us-problems of the highways, problems of alcohol and all the heartache and sorrow they bring, as well as the bail provisions-but in the interests of time I shall deal only with that part of the bill relating to sexual offences.
I have no complaint about the substance of these amendments and I am most anxious that the bill move into committee where there will be the opportunity for questioning and applying some flexibility. I should like to find out what prompted the wording of some of these amendments, and where the government intends to go with them; what threat they feel the amendments will answer in our society. What concerns me about this bill and many of its predecessors to amend the code is the lack of responsiveness or responsibility to come to grips with the whole spectrum of sexual offences.
Yesterday, the minister spoke of this bill as being part of a series of measures that would be responsive to a real, genuine concern of Canadians. I agree absolutely. He spoke of an ongoing review of the Criminal Code to reflect the changing attitudes of Canadians. I agree with that. We have to be responsive. When people are fearful of bodily harm or of property damage, we as legislators have to be responsive to those genuine concerns. I agree with the four aspects that prompted this legislation. The minister spoke, first, of the need to develop updated information; second, of the need to respond to the recent prevalence of certain crimes; third, of the need to deal with persistent problems that recent attempts had not been successful with; and, finally, he spoke of the need to modernize procedures. I agree that all of this is responsive government action.
This has happened with the Criminal Code for years. I can only refer to it as a patchwork of certain areas. We are responsive to that particular action whether it be because of pressure in our constituencies, interest groups bringing it to our attention, or any number of other sources of pressure put upon us. What I question when I read a bill like this is the responsibility of this reaction. I am not saying that the bill is irresponsible. I do not say that at all. I question whether there is the responsibility that is necessary in this type of reaction. What is lacking, in my opinion, is the responsibility to deal with the larger prob-


lem. The hon. member for Lotbiniere dealt with that. In the area of sexual offences, we are dealing with only three or four offences.
In my opinion, more responsible action, rather than a responsive reaction, is called for in dealing with this part of the code. I do not confine that observation to sexual offences but I think it happens to be a rather good one. It happens to be the one we are dealing with in Bill C-71. I have had limited experience in the criminal courts. I practised criminal law for a while and thought I knew a little bit about it. When preparing for this debate, I was amazed at the vast variety and number of sexual offences contained in the Canadian Criminal Code. Some are specifically crimes against women. In other words, the sex of the victim is what we look for in search of that provision in the code which prohibits a certain form of behaviour. Others are simple crimes, unacceptable behaviour. It is the nature of the behaviour rather than the victim either directly or by implication being sexual behaviour.
Statistics Canada lists 14 categories of sexual offences. These are not individual offences, but categories. I am not an individual who becomes enthralled by statistics, but I could not help noting in the Statistics Canada report which covers three years-1969, 1970 and 1971-that in two of those years, 1969 and 1970, there were only nine of the 14 categories in which more than 15 convictions were secured in that calendar year. In 1971, the third year covered in the report, there were only seven categories with more than 15 convictions. I find it rather remarkable that there were numerous categories of sex crimes in which 15 or less convictions were registered in any year.
At the other end of the scale is the relatively high number of convictions in one or two categories. I find that in the category of indecent assault on a female there is roughly double the number of convictions than in any other category. I think we can draw only one conclusion if we look at this question intelligently and objectively: this charge has become a catch-all; it is a basket clause for all clauses where we cannot register convictions for much more serious crimes. When there is any doubt about how the Crown prosecutor will proceed with regard to a sex crime, he will proceed with indecent assault on a female person. In my opinion, the incentive which must exist to do that indicates there is something basically and seriously wrong with the Criminal Code in this particular area.
Second, the Statistics Canada report impressed me by the fact that there were extremely low conviction rates in many areas compared with the number of charges laid. In terms of percentage, in many cases there was well below a 50 per cent conviction rate. On the other hand, on the specific charge of indecent assault against a female, the conviction rate was between 75 per cent and 85 per cent. Again, something has to be seriously wrong when within this group of 14 categories we find that in 1971 there was only a 48 per cent conviction rate for attempted rape, 42 per cent for corrupting morals, and 49 per cent for rape, while indecent assault on a female or indecent assault on a male had a 75 per cent conviction rate. There is something inherently and basically wrong with that structure when we have such a variety not only in terms of number of
Criminal Code
convictions but in terms of convictions based on the total number of charges laid.
Third, the Statistics Canada report reveals that except for convictions for rape and procuring, over 50 per cent of convicted sexual offenders were either fined or given suspended sentences. I find it very difficult to determine the reason for this, particularly having in mind the maximum sentences that these various charges carry. The maximum sentences that can be imposed at the discretion of the judge are extremely high, yet over 50 per cent of the cases, with the exception of rape and procuring, resulted in fines or suspended sentences. I cannot reconcile all these very compelling statistics. They indicate that at least one section of offences under the code is not operating in the way one would expect. What concerns me on this last point of 50 per cent being fined or given suspended sentences is the possibility-I go no further than that-that our courts do not attach that degree of seriousness to these offences which one would expect of the judiciary, especially in light of the maximum sentences judges are capable of imposing for convictions under these sections.
I might also refer the minister to the Statistics Canada report which is entitled "Statistics of criminal and other offences, 1969, 1970 and 1971". In particular, I would ask that he note the rather substantial number of charges for indictable offences that were reduced to lesser offences. All of us who have practised in the criminal courts are familiar with the situation of plea bargaining, for example, where one is able to convince a Crown attorney to proceed on a lesser offence. In this particular area, however, I am astounded at the number. I do not wish to quote the statistics; they are available to the minister and his departmental officials. I am referring to cases reduced from indictable offences to lesser offences. All of this makes me wonder whether the Criminal Code is really in touch with the realities of the seventies.
I have to wonder when, if ever, the minister and his department will come to grips with the over-all problem of dealing effectively with the whole range of sexual offences or the whole range of other offences in the code. There are several offences against property, offences against the person, and so on. Let me confine myself to this aspect today, namely, sexual offences.
I am very impressed with the material I received from the Law Reform Commission. However, I am afraid I have been impressed before. I have read reports that have come to grips with the very difficult, over-all problems. As a practising lawyer, I have never been the beneficiary of any approach by government at the federal level other than a patchwork one desperately trying to keep our code up to date. In other words, I ask the minister at some stage to resist the historical tradition of this approach to the code.
I suggest, in all seriousness, that certain law school classes-I think specifically of criminal law and evidence classes-occupy a very large percentage of their time with the professor pointing out to the students the anomalies, inconsistencies and contradictions that inevitably are available to such a professor because we have approached our criminal justice for such a long time in the manner I have described.
In looking through the Statistics Canada figures, I wonder why we still have a provision for the offence of


Criminal Code
seduction of female passengers on board vessels. I think it is still in there. It certainly was in 1971. I am sure at one time it may have been necessary. I can imagine the period of large immigration of young women coming to Canada to work as domestics, being away from home, without protection of any kind, on a very long and difficult sea voyage from Europe to Canada. Maybe at that time it was essential that something be done, although I rather doubt it; I think other sections could have covered it. Why, in the seventies, we should be preoccupied about the seduction of female passengers aboard vessels is something which escapes me.
There are other provisions we should be questioning. Rather than reacting to the difficulties of society in a somewhat reactionary manner, we should be working out more positive responses. Why should we be so concerned about sexual intercourse with a female employee or with the seduction of a female between 16 and 18? Surely there are other parts of the code capable of dealing with this type of behaviour. When I look at the section covering seduction of female passengers on vessels, I think it would be more pertinent to worry about the seduction of female passengers on motor bikes, or hitch-hikers. If we want to regulate, let us do so with regard to female passengers on motor bikes, and female hitch-hikers. I do not think we should be reacting; I think we should be acting.
I am afraid the code is a series of regulations which display little leadership. There are many things we can discuss in committee. There are questions to be answered, and possibly some amendments to be made to these amendments. I hope that at some stage we shall begin dealing with things that are a little more pertinent. I have to ask myself and my colleagues in this Chamber, what is "previous chaste character"? Is it credibility we are looking for? In four sections of the code, if I am correct, the words "of previous chaste character" are operative words for the court to consider. I have to ask myself why this is in the code. There are, obviously, certain circumstances in which credibility, pattern of behaviour, or any number of things may be interpreted in the light of previous chaste behaviour, but surely we need not make operative words such as "of previous chaste character" of such importance.
Again, I wonder why, except in rather remarkable circumstances, we should identify the sex of a victim. Indecent assault of a female is one thing; indecent assault of a male is in another section. I ask myself why we are so preoccupied with identifying the sex of a victim. There may be occasions upon which this is necessary, but if we agree with this type of wording, why should the sex of the animal not be specified in offences involving bestiality? It is as absurd as that. I would hope that when changes are forthcoming in response to the work of the Law Reform Commission or otherwise, the minister will come to grips with that sort of question.
With respect to Bill C-71 as it deals with rape and related offences, we are dealing of course with myths, as we always do. The myth is that a "bad woman" is incapable of being raped. The hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) dealt very effectively with this aspect yesterday. We have to deal with the myth that the credibility of a "bad woman" is immediately in question. I was never sure

what that phrase meant. As a lawyer, all I knew was that it was of benefit to hurl as much dirt as possible in the direction of such a woman, hoping that some of it would stick and that the jury would disbelieve what she said. We avoid making a value judgment as to what is good or what is bad; we simply try to paint her bad or good without asking ourselves what is good or what is bad in today's society.
I am just trying to help the minister because I have a great deal of respect for him. I hope he will not be tempted to follow a course based on reaction but, rather, that he will act positively to lead the code in directions which are not only more practical and more realistic but more in keeping with the integrity of the House, of the department and of our fellow Canadians.
I shall not deal specifically with the various sections. On second reading I would prefer, rather, to generalize. I wonder whether the minister should not be thinking of completely eliminating the offence of rape. When I consider all the aspects the Crown must prove in a rape case, I can think of behaviour which lacks those certain elements but which might be far more offensive to the victim, or to society, than rape. One important part of a rape case is proof of penetration. I can think of behaviour toward a victim which is far more dangerous than that-although it is, of course, a serious matter.
My hon. friend from Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) said yesterday that perhaps we should be thinking in different terms. I suggest this to the minister for whatever it is worth: I wonder whether in this whole area we should not be thinking in terms of assault rather than intercourse. After all, that is the nature of a rape case; it is intercourse by assault. If you can prove there has been no assault, you can prove consent, which is a good defence. If we really wanted to come to grips with this area of the code, we would be thinking in terms of assault. The nature and the degree of the assault would be reflected in the sentence. If it were a horrendous assault resulting in grievous bodily harm, that would be dealt with in terms of the sentence. The crime would be criminal assault on a male or a female. I do not know why we should not consider that aspect. It is not necessary that bodily harm result, though, again, if bodily harm did not result that would be pertinent to the sentence imposed on persons committing such offences. I very much question whether it matters whether the victim is a male or a female. I think we should be directing our minds to these points.
Mr. Speaker, I have taken more time than I had intended, but I feel strongly about these matters and I appreciate the opportunity to make a contribution. These amendments, regarded in a very narrow light, are good. They are another in a series of amendments that have been made over the years. If we continue our present course, I suggest our successors will likely see the same amendments 20 or 30 years from now. I hope that in his new portfolio, in which I sincerely wish him well, the minister will regard the Criminal Code, not as legislation that should be patched, plugged, enlarged or restricted but, rather, as a great challenge, one that the minister is capable of coming to grips with. Speaking for myself, I look forward to the time when legislation is introduced, not dealing with iso-


lated amendments to the code but demonstrating a really genuine and new approach to criminal justice in Canada.

speechtext:
This may be a way of curtailing consumption of gasoline because the police would not have to do very much driving: they could just park at the one place and wait for the customers to come to them. I suppose they do this in regard to bawdy houses. That is why the police do not like freelancers on the street, because they have to go and look for them rather than standing outside the bawdy house waiting for the men to go in and then raiding the place.
It seems to me the minister is doing a lot of things, in response to public demand for law and order, that really will not create law and order. It seems to me that many of these things favour the police and do nothing for the individual. I am sure if you asked people in this country how they felt about prohibition, you would find they were not in favour of it; yet they might agree to allow the police to sit outside our hotels arresting everybody who came out onto the street. That is an exaggeration, but that is what appears to be said in these amendments.
We have had great difficulty in providing any kind of defence to the breathalyzer. I remember suggesting on a number of occasions when the breathalyzer legislation was brought in that there be a method provided allowing the defendant a breathalyzer sample for his own use. You will remember that the then minister of justice, the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Turner) promised that when a breathalyzer sample was taken, a sample would be provided for the use of the defence. To my knowledge, that has never been successful and has been discontinued.
What we are really saying in this legislation is that these people on the road are guilty, so the police might just as


well take along a receipt book and collect the fines. With the changes proposed in this legislation, they might just as well confiscate the cars and take the drivers down to the hoosegow, because they are going to receive a sentence in any case. I think the public should know that, or should be aware of the fact that this is exactly what is going to happen under this legislation. That is why I am opposed to it.
There are many changes proposed that are necessary and worth while, and we should congratulate the minister for them. I am not particularly bothered by the clause in respect of cattle rustling. I think it is amusing that we should go back 100 years and insert a special provision to prohibit cattle rustling. However, I am completely in agreement with those who maintain it is a very serious problem, even if some people derive quite a good living from it. It is a serious offence. The offence is always related to the price of the animal. There is difficulty involved in meeting the normal requirements of proof when only the insides of the animal are left in someone's field.
There are some interesting offences. One which I believe deserves an explanation from the minister is the one concerning begging. I would think the minister would be ashamed to include such a clause in Canadian legislation. When we have to legislate in the way they do in India or in some of the near East countries to prohibit begging, then I think we should do something about unemployment and the payments paid to welfare recipients so that this would no longer necessary. When we find it necessary to write legislation, in 1975, to prohibit begging, this says something about our society which would be better left unsaid.
There is another clause in which I am interested, although I am not qualified to speak on it and I hope no other member of this House is. It involves the problem of detention of the mentally ill. It relates both sentencing and the question of whether or nor these individuals should be tried. In my area, I have found quite often that the psychiatrists to whom these people are sent are crazier than the people sent to them. Often these people could be certified under any definition we might use. I know some of them. They would not meet any of the criteria a normal person would use in determining sanity. I know a young lad in my riding who had a serious problem. He was sent to Penetanguishene. When he returned, his doctor informed me that the would probably never be normal again. We sent him there for examination, and that is what happened to him while he was there. It seems to me this situation is often repeated.
Places like Penetanguishene would be very good places in which to produce horror movies. There probably are not too many places where one would find the kind of people who are in charge of such institutions. The people in these institutions to which we refer people are not the types who can do anything for them. I respect the judge who is sympathetic with these people, who remands them for examination and then sends them to places where he hopes something can be done for them in the way of assistance, so that they will come back with a recommendation for further care which will eliminate the need for a trial in respect of the offence they may have committed. Then
Criminal Code
there are judges who sentence people for a period of more than two years simply so that they will be able to get them into a federal institution where they can obtain psychiatric help. I have visited many of these institutions and I believe that such a judge is misguided. I believe more serious consideration should be given to this matter.
There are good institutions. I think particularly of the Clark clinic in Toronto. It has a very good reputation. Unfortunately, it is not one of the institutions to which people can be sent by a court. This institution has done remarkable work with disturbed people. It is the kind of institution to which I believe judges think they are sending people.
In this bill we are making a number of amendments concerning the mentally ill. I believe this to be one of the worst problems we have in our whole criminal structure. In this regard, I do not believe we are able to obtain the type of advice that is needed for our courts, our prosecutors or the defence. When a person is sentenced, he is frequently sent to a place at which he will receive absolutely no assistance in correcting his mental difficulty. In many cases, the difficulty will merely be accentuated because of loneliness, frustration, segregation and the other things which quite often are the fate of those committed to penitentiaries because of unacceptable, antisocial crimes.
It is right that we should try, in respect of the Criminal Code, to correct some of these things in relation to the mentally ill; but if there are no suitable institutions to which people could be sent, then it seems to me we are merely satisfying our own conscience by passing this legislation. I am sure that any lawyer in this House who has had anything to do with criminal law, and has seen a person committed to our mental institutions, knows full well that such an individual is being sent into a situation which will cause the deterioration of his condition and certainly will not help him overcome the anti-social condition he had which took him out of society in the first place.
One matter which has not received attention in this bill is that of adjournments. Sometimes when a person is charged with a small offence and attends court, he finds that the defence lawyer is not feeling good on that day and adjourns the case. Such a person has the expense involved of bringing his witnesses again and hiring a lawyer. The next time he attends court, perhaps in another two weeks, the Crown prosecutor may stand up and ask for an adjournment because he has a golf game or some other important activity. On another occasion, the judge may decide that he does not want to hear the case at that time because his holidays are coming up. Believe me, this happens very regularly during the summer. In some instances a case is adjourned for two months.
It seems to me that when many of these cases are adjourned for periods of eight or ten weeks, justice is not being done, it is not seen to be done, and in my opinion it is being abused by those who are supposed to protect the judicial system. I am quite sure there are legitimate reasons for cases being adjourned, but I do not think the excuses I have heard on a number of occasions in court are legitimate excuses which warrant bringing the person charged back into the court week after week at considerable expense, and sometimes at the loss of his job.

I have mentioned that some of the provisions in this bill, I believe, are the result of overreaction on the part of lawyers to a legitimate call for law and order. I also think that a number of things were left out which should perhaps be in this bill. But I hope that members of parliament will not consider it necessary to tighten the laws to such an extent that the rights of the ordinary citizen are jeopardized and he is penalized for actions which he takes which are not detrimental to society.
A great deal has been said in the last few days about drinking drivers. I am impressed with the amount of my money that the insurance company is spending to carry out surveys to find out how many accidents have been alcohol-related. I have paid for these surveys. I have not had an accident for a long time, but my accident insurance goes up and up, partly because the insurance company is trying to protect itself rather than doing something about problems over which they may have some control, one of these being the issuance of large sums of insurance money in the payment of claims, which allows people to drive when they should not be driving.
The insurance companies know very well why they collect such large premiums, and they have control over that money. It is also a fact that drunken drivers have been the cause of far too many fatalities. But I suggest that our criteria are wrong. A police officer judges the situation when he sees a car going off the white line or wandering over the road, the driver driving erratically or behaving in an abnormal way. This warrants the stopping of that car and allows the policeman to ask the driver to step out, and if he has reasonable grounds to suspect the person may be under the influence of alcohol he will take him for a breathalyzer test, against which there is almost no defence.
We did not supply the police with the means with which to test drivers on the spot, but we accept the results of the breathalyzer machine and that becomes the overriding factor upon which to convict the driver. However, the police officer need not observe any unusual behaviour; all we require is that if a driver is stopped and refuses to take a breathalyzer test, regardless of whether he has been drinking he is arrested and may be convicted. Even if there has been no abnormal behaviour and a person is observed only to have left a party, a beer parlour or some function where alcoholic beverages were served, the police officer may wait until the man steps into his car and before he even drives it can require him to take a breathalyzer test and arrest him if he refuses. That may be a great way of raising revenue for the police force, but it seems to me the minister should be fair and should provide the public with some protection against such things as speed traps and the kind of trap I have just described, both of which are permitted under our judicial system and are designed to fleece the public.
Everyone in this country agrees that if a person is unduly under the influence of alcohol so that his judgment and driving ability are affected, he should not be driving. But we do not ask him what his IQ is, and we know there are people who have driving licences whose IQ is very low and whose reactions are very slow. Some very good drivers who have more than the permissible level of alcohol in their blood are able to function much better than some
people who have taken no alcohol. I watched some tests this summer of people who had taken drugs or alcohol, highly qualified drivers who drove cars on the track under controlled circumstances. It was surprising to see that those people did a lot better, even after taking large doses of drugs or alcohol, than most of us in this chamber could do, because they were highly skilled drivers and for them to be half capable still meant they could drive much better than most people.
So I suggest that we should not get carried away and pass laws without providing any defence for the ordinary citizen. We should not take away the rights of an individual on the whim of a police officer. It seems to me that the breathalyzer test is a terrible law and lawyers should be opposed to it. I have spoken to many lawyers, including Arthur Martin, whom I consider to be perhaps the greatest criminal lawyer in Ontario. He agrees that the ordinary citizen has no defence in these cases and that this is deplorable. He said it is unfortunate that we have not been able to develop any kind of equality between prosecution and defence in breathalyzer-test cases and in the operation and supervision of tests, and that we have been unable to give the defence a decent break. The law now extends to drivers who have more than two beers and it would apply even, I am sure, to most members of parliament who visit Your Honour's quarters on occasion and are served refreshments, following which they drive home. Yet we are the people who will vote.
