Mr. Speaker, having been a member of the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs since I became an MP in 1968, I am pleased to take part in this debate, not to lengthen it, nor to make revolutionary suggestions, but merely to voice my frank and sincere views on the proposed amendments.
The bill amending the Criminal Code is one among several others which are part of the permanent review of the Criminal Code, a necessary operation-as regards substance, procedure and evidence-to take into consideration



the development of outlooks and create more effective means to control crime.
It is also seen as an opportunity to assess the results of recent amendments and bring further alterations. Increasingly, criminality takes an international turn. The amendments concerning conspiracy and the laundering of illegal income deal with that problem. Some practices of our modern way of life involve the increasing use of credit cards, which incites and even compels the legislator to attack specifically such problems as theft or fraudulent use of credit cards and swindling in matters of telecommunication.
Mr. Speaker, the amendments introduced at the present time are the result of various cases of some specific problems that have risen and in others, the awareness that the existing provisions have become outdated. These amendments, whose purpose is to remedy some problems that have already risen or that are expected, follow to a large extent the recommendations made by the criminal law section of the conference on uniform legislation, by the Canadian Bar Association, the provincial attorneys general, police departments and the general public opinion. Therefore, it is a participation process involving all segments of the population. Besides, the works of the Law Reform Commission will very likely lead to new recommendations along this line.
The bill now before us, Mr. Speaker, is only one of a series of bills introduced in recent years to update the Criminal Code. To me this updating is necessary if we want the Crimianl Code to remain an effective instrument of control in an ever-changing society.
I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, that the proposed amendments aim at making the code provisions clearer and more precise where there have been difficulties. One of the most obvious areas is that of bail. The main purpose of the Bail Reform Act enacted in 1972 was to prevent an accused from being detained under guard without real necessity before his trial. However, it was soon realized there was an obvious need to make some provisions harsher so as to close the door to abuses capable of jeopardizing the consistency of the pre-trial release system. The general rule remains the same. When someone is arrested and appears before the judge, he must be released on bail unless the Crown gives the judge convincing reasons in favour of his detention. The changes are important, however, for in some cases they hold the accused rather than the Crown responsible for proving that public interest does not warrant temporary detention. Such could be the case of an accused who is waiting for his trial for a previous criminal act, after having abused the liberal provisions of the parole system.
The provisions governing driving while under the influence should be further defined and strengthened. Under the current provisions of the Criminal Code, a police officer cannot demand a breath sample unless he has reasonable and probable cause to believe that the driving ability of an operator is impaired, which is practically without effect, and except for breathalizer tests which, under a number of provincial statutes, law enforcement officers may carry out on the spot and at random, they cannot take preventive measures to discover delinquents.
Criminal Code
Alcoholic drivers are a serious and constant threat on our highways. That is why the amendments proposed today would authorize the police to make road controls, to track down possible law breakers, when an agent has reason to suspect that a person is driving in a state of drunkenness. Of course, we will need the co-operation of the police forces if those amendments are not to be used to the detriment of the population. But I feel we must show confidence in those who are entrusted with the heavy responsibility of keeping order, and who have to use their judgment every time circumstances warrant it.
Mr. Speaker, another objective of the bill is to introduce in the penal code provisions to deal with the crimes that make the headlines in our society. The increase in international gangsterism creates a serious problem for our own forces. That is why we must change our Criminal Code.
Whoever has in his possession what he knows to have been obtained fraudulently commits a crime. However, that provision applies strictly to the object that was stolen, not to whatever it has been transformed into later on.
The amendment introduced today and which I fully support provides that it is illegal in Canada to be in possession of goods or proceeds while knowing that they were obtained by criminal offences committed either in Canada or in foreign countries. This amendment is meant to prevent the entry in Canada of forged goods stolen or illegally procured, but touched up, and to strengthen law enforcement forces in their fight against international gangsterism.
What is the most important, in my opinion, in the proposed amendments, is to update certain parts of the Criminal Code to catch up with the change in the way of thinking of the public. Under the amendments discussed in the House, electric billiards machines, which dispense as prizes free games, are excluded from the group of prohibited slot machines.
This change in the way of thinking, Mr. Speaker, is reflected in the provisions of the Criminal Code dealing with electric billiards and lotteries.
Mr. Speaker, it is important to recall that in Quebec, games of chance play an important role and are a source of income for a great many people. Now, Mr. Speaker, if a man in Ontario operated a slot machine and was charged, he was fined but the machine was not seized. In Quebec, in similar cases, not only did the offender pay the fine, but the machine was seized, so much so that people in Quebec were being discriminated against and yet they were not operating the slot machines in a more illegal way than people in Ontario.
This provision, Mr. Speaker, will allow people in Quebec to operate the machines and it will create and protect a substantial number of jobs. I know what I am talking about for having been appoached by many people to make representations in order that the legislation be extended to allow Quebecers to take advantage legally and normally of the games of chance, legally controlled. Of course, abuse should be avoided and people should not be encouraged to spend their salaries in games, but there is still a mentality in Quebec which we should respect, and this is to spend large amounts of money on games. Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a personal remark and oppose one of the


Criminal Code
provisions in this bill. One of the amendments is aimed at removing corroboration in the case of rape.
I would like to speak strongly against this amendment which I think is not realistic. As attorney for the defence, I had the opportunity, on several occasions, Mr. Speaker, to attend trials with people charged with rape. I had the occasion to face one of the most perfect scenarios prepared by Crown attorneys who urged their clients to wear the most sexy clothes of course, as they were women. A scenario whose purpose is unfairly to influence the jury which from the outset is sympathetic to the woman in the witness box who has been the victim of the abuse. There is, in my view, in that kind of trial, an implicit condemnation of the accused and by removing the corroboration requirement we would place the accused in an unfavourable position to the extent that the basic principle of our legal system, namely that the accused must be presumed innocent until proven guilty, would practically no longer exist.
I grant you, Mr. Speaker, that it may be difficult for a person who has his first experience in court to express himself easily, to present his problem in a thorough and fair manner, and that, in case of a rape, the victim must be given the chance to explain her case and be protected by the law. But that is a long way from placing the accused in jeopardy. I think the bill goes much too far and does not take certain situations into account, all the more so since rape victims have often placed themselves in a situation which invited the attack. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope I will not take too much of the time of the House, but I am interested in two aspects of the bill and I want to address myself to two particular clauses. I will keep within the Speaker's injunction of not particularizing at this general stage. I want to pay some attention to clause 75; I suppose one might term it the Morgentaler appeal provision. Obviously, the case of Dr. Morgentaler is the reason for this change in the Criminal Code. I congratulate not only the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) but the former minister under whose auspices this essential reform is placed before us.
It is a very fascinating study to look at the Criminal Code and try to discover why Canada got itself into this position relative to appeal procedure. I asked the library of parliament to look at this question when the issue had so much publicity some months ago; then I had some research done by Mr. Arthur Blakely of the Montreal Gazette, who wrote a most interesting column on the subject in the July 2 issue. It was found that this provision in the Criminal Code came about without any debate at all in parliament. I think one member, Mr. Tommy Church of Toronto, objected to the provision. It came about under the auspices of a liberal-both capital and small "1"-member, the late Mr. Ernest Lapointe, minister of justice. As far as we were able to discover in research, parliament passed it without any comment at all.
The origin was in the 1923 amendment to the Criminal Code when the provision for narcotics offences was inserted. The provision was that there would be no appeal. This is a very cursory and rather simplistic comment at this stage of the debate, but years before, in Britain, a criminal court of appeal was set up. As was usual in those days, Canada lagged behind substantially: in criminal cases there was no appeal procedure. Senator McMeans of Winnipeg should be honoured by the Law Society of Manitoba for getting the then government to amend the law and provide for an appeal procedure. In any event, the government bought the package. I am sorry I am falling into using contemporary cliche. I determined that I would never use the word "package," but I find it all around me. We have packages of housing and packages of law. Here I am, caught in the same cliche.
In any event, the amendments were approved by parliament. As I understand it, until the Morgentaler case no court ever reversed a jury's verdict. If I am not correct about this, I hope that at a later stage somebody will tell me so. I hope I am not inflexible. The government has now seen fit to deal with what, more than civil libertarians, anybody who has an interest in law reform must have seen as a serious aberration in the law.
I want publicly to pay tribute to Mr. Blakely for his column and historical research. I hope one day the Law Society of Manitoba will in some way remember a senator


who did something that a government was not prepared to do except as a compromise back in 1930, namely, having an appeal procedure.
I want to refer, as many of my colleagues have already, to the sections dealing with sexual offences, rape in particular. With the greatest respect to a person for whom I have great admiration-the previous speaker-I feel, and I hope we can talk about this at the committee stage, that it is insulting to the victim of rape to say, as I believe he did, that in many instances she is asking for it. This is one of the oldest slanders on women. I am surprised that an otherwise progressive member would fall into the trap. It is an old one, it is an ugly one, and it is one that I personally deplore.
Lord Chief Justice Matthew Hale, the famous seventeenth century English jurist, assured himself of immortality when he wrote the words, "Rape is an accusation easily to be made and hard to be proved, and harder to be defended by the party accused, though never so innocent." The trouble with the jurisprudence in this part of the law is that most people would agree with the seventeenth century chief justice. I suggest he was wrong. Rape is, indeed, a most vicious crime. I do not for one minute say that my hon. friend thought otherwise; I just meant that his attitude about victims was wrong.
Four out of five rapes go unreported. It is fair to say categorically that women do not find rape an accusation easily to be made, despite the chief justice who in his time and place was reflecting attitudes of a government of a couple of hundred years ago. Those who do report their rape soon find, however, that it is indeed hard for it to be proved. We have extensive records to show that this is the case. By and large, a successful legal defence is rather easy.
This quotation is from a horrible book-horrible in its statistical data but a very powerful expose on the history of rape. It is called "Against our Will", written by Susan Brownmiller. It is a very contemporary book that was just received by our library. She wrote that the law requires that you examine with caution the testimony of the female person named in the information. There is the injunction that is slanderous, or bordering upon slander. There is no other crime of which I am aware where the deponent is not believed or needs support. However, in the case of rape a man usually does not believe the person; therefore, all sorts of unpleasantness results in the trial. I quote from the book:
That the testimony of the female person should be examined with caution is the bottom line in all rape cases from the moment they are reported to that rarer moment, if ever, when they are actually brought to trial...
To a woman the definition of rape is fairly simple. A sexual invasion of the body by force, an incursion into the private, personal inner space without consent. .. constitutes a deliberate violation of emotional, physical and rational integrity and is a hostile, degrading act of violence that deserves the name of rape.
The fact that many people have been able to speak about this subject freely is a healthy sign. This has been after a good deal of persuasion, mostly by women and, in a very dramatic way, by the Royal Commission on the Status of Women and the Advisory Council on the Status of Women. A great deal of supporting documents have been prepared, for example by M. H. Rioux and others, and all have raised our consciousness about the subject.
Criminal Code
I congratulate the government for making a move, but I am saddened by the fact that the move is not the reform called for by the Law Reform Commission. The Law Reform Commission said that the matter of the woman's character should not be relevant in a rape case. I, for one, would have supported the minister had he seen fit to go to that extent.
I have just a couple of other comments to make. One is the interesting discussion by a very modern, contemporary judge, Edson Haines of the high court of Ontario, in Chit-ty's Law Journal of February, 1975. Mr. Justice Haines, in summary, felt a good deal of improvement could be made, not only as the minister proposes but in the attitudes of the various attorneys general and their Crown prosecutors. I hope the fact that in many of our larger cities, rape crisis centres are being established is a positive thing. I also believe that in every case where a woman is laying a charge or laying information, a woman should be present. Most of our police forces now have women police officers and this is something the municipal police forces and the RCMP could very well do.
The code changes must be supported, when parliament adopts the minister's bill, by a change in procedures, a change in our attitude toward this crime. The attitude of many people is that this is just another event in a person's life; it is tragic; it will be a nuisance to try to catch the perpetrator of the crime, and it is all part of the indignity done to women. Witness the newsstands today. I am, heaven knows, no advocate of censorship, but I think there are instances when our respect for one half of the population, or over one half of the population, should lead us to want to exorcise this evil from our newsstands. It is really one of the most insulting things which can be done to a woman.
At any rate, I hope that with this mini-reform-I call it that; I think the minister could have gone a little further; he could have accepted the recommendations of the Law Reform Commission-the attitude of the police, Crown prosecutors and men in general will undergo a fundamental change. I hope many of my colleagues will see fit to try to get from the library Susan Brownmiller's book, because it tells a terrible story, I am. sorry it has taken so many years, in parliamentary terms and in terms of civility, to recognize rape for what it is.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first time, I believe, on which I have had occasion to address the new Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada (Mr. Basford) in his new capacity. I should like to express my congratulations to him on assuming this position. I think it is an honour for any member of the bar to be named to such an important portfolio. It is particularly important now, when, as the minister himself said as he opened the debate, concern for the whole question of the prevention and detection of crime and decent security in our country is a matter of great public importance in the minds of Canadians. He also said Canadians have a right to enjoy a sense of safety on the streets and in their homes and cities, a right which has long been a hallmark of our country's way of life. I use exactly the words the minister used in the opening of his


Criminal Code
speech. I think it is important that that be said, because whether we like it or not-and as a lawyer I do not like it-there is a feeling in Canada that perhaps in terms of the administration of justice we have got a bit out of balance.
Perhaps that feeling is caused by the fact that there is a feeling sentences are not long enough, that the administration of justice in terms of penalties is not harsh enough in terms of the realities of Canadian life. Perhaps it has been brought about by the fact that our criminal law is codified. A number of things could have caused this impression. I shall not be partisan, because there will be other occasions when we shall be dealing with other matters and we shall say things about the importance of the administration of justice. Perhaps it is caused, as well, by the fact that we tend nowadays to look, in terms of the administration of justice and the administration of the criminal law, to the causes of crime rather than to the penalties for crime.
For some reason it has gotten about in society that a penalty is not a deterrent. I cannot bring myself to accept that view. It seems, having taken that position, that we have tended to overemphasize the importance of the crowding of the cities, the depletion of good housing and all the other social factors which we say somehow or other make it not necessarily the fault of the perpetrator of the crime. That is the impression, and I think it is a very dangerous impression. I am happy that this bill will go some way toward changing it.
I have no doubt that those things cause a lowering of social conditions and perhaps breed attitudes which cannot be combated by our treatment of perpetrators of criminal conduct, but there is a danger that in some respects, in terms of the administration of the law, we are getting further and further away from the principle that a man or a woman is responsible for his or her conduct, and that if the norms of society are breached there is a penalty to be paid. Perhaps what I am trying to say is that, in terms of the administration of justice, we are perhaps confusing the problem of the rehabilitation of the prisoner with the protection of society.
I, for one, think it is not brutalizing to say that the emphasis ought to be upon the protection of society. That is why we are having demands for gun control; it is not just because of past events. It is why we are taking a more harsh look at capital punishment and a number of other matters. It is just as much part of law reform-and this bill is one with respect to law reform-that we recognize that the enforcement of the law and that the penalties provided for breach of the law fit the crime and the criminal, and it is to this that the court must address itself. An old Scottish judge once said, "Show me the man and I will interpret the law". I think we should consider the wisdom of this ancient Scottish judge who many years ago spoke in that way.
Another matter that is not within the federal jurisdiction but which nonetheless is important to us when we consider any reformation of the law is this. Not only should justice be swift, it should be sure. It should be also fair in terms of what the criminal as well as society can expect as a result of the commission of a certain crime. I

think this is what the hon. member for Perth-Wilmot (Mr. Jarvis) was getting at when he said, in speaking of the offence of rape and related offences, that really they are all assaults and that we ought to examine the sentences we prescribe for the different kinds of assaults that there are.
I remember speaking to a retired military officer who had presided at many courts martial and appeals from courts martial. He told me that there was no question in his mind, from his experience-which was as great as any judge educated in the law in any province in this country-that there is a deterrent effect if one knows that breach of what are rules of conduct is going to lead (a) to a charge, (b) to a conviction, (c) to punishment fitting the crime, and that this is swift and sure.
One of the problems that was pointed out to me by a provincial court judge in our city, a man young in years but wise in terms of experience, is that what happens in this country generally is that between the time a man is charged with a crime and the final disposition of the trial some six to nine months elapse. This becomes important in considering the effect of bail laws. Our bail laws have been interpreted as saying that, subject to certain conditions, an accused has the right to walk free. We cannot consider the operation of the bail laws without considering the operation of the courts. When a person accused of a crime is then allowed to walk free, police officers with whom I am acquainted have told me that many crimes are committed by people on bail. I should like to see some statistics in this regard and I hope we will have some to consider when we deal with the bill in committee.
I am not suggesting that the slowness of the courts system is the fault of the Attorney General of Canada, because it is not his jurisdiction. I am merely saying that, in considering the way in which we are to interpret the bail law or how the bail laws should read, we should recognize that in terms of the operation of the courts and administration of justice in all of the provinces of this country there is a slowness today which not only can lead to the walking of the streets by people likely to commit offences, but which offers no deterrent since the administration of justice is not swift and sure. I think these are matters we will have to consider as we go down the road and deal with this bill.
I understand the minister wants to speak and close this debate, but I should just like to turn to one other matter raised in the course of the speech of the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters). The hon. member spoke about the road testing provisions of this bill and said they were an invasion of people's civil rights, that they did something to the operation of the criminal law in Canada. With great respect to him, I think he is wrong. In considering this question, the most important aspect has to be public safety.
I look upon the provisions proposed in the legislation as an extension of the public's concern not so much for the person who uses an automobile while his ability to control it is impaired, but for the safety of the person with whom the driver may come into contact. The number of deaths, injuries and maimings resulting from the combination of alcohol and automobile driving is such that we cannot deny that, without some additional protection beyond that which we now have, the public safety will be neglected, and the Attorney General of Canada could be criticized for


Criminal Code
much crime has gone unnoticed. Generally speaking, I hope I am regarded as progressive in terms of the law. I have had the honour to practice in this city for a number of years. I think most members of the bar are inclined to look at the law as a living thing. I think they are also inclined to say from time to time that legislatures do not move fast enough to keep up with the dynamics of society. This is an attempt by the Attorney General and his predecessor to do that, and to the extent they have done so, which I think is reasonable, I look forward to the committee hearings on this bill.
In closing, I want again to commend the Attorney General on his appointment and to wish him well in a portfolio which is extremely important to every Canadian.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to take only a few minutes to present one or two points in respect of Bill C-71. I understand there is a disposition to give the bill second reading before we adjourn today. First, I should like to commend the minister for bringing in Bill C-71 and specifically the provisions relating to sex-related crimes and to rape in particular. I recall a lady coming into my office a few weeks ago and describing her experience and the difficulties she faced at the preliminary hearing and those she would be facing immediately after that. I commend the minister for taking a look at this serious problem and bringing in provisions regarding these crimes.
I want to speak very briefly on the provisions in the bill relating to interprovincial lotteries. One might say that the whole matter of the acceptability by the public of lotteries is a foregone conclusion. If we want to measure the success of lotteries in terms of participation in the Olympic lottery or, for that matter, the western Canadian lottery, I suppose we might find that they are very well received. I should like to present to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) one or two points of view. I seriously question whether at this time-I am not trying to be negative with regard to the bill, but I would like to present the concern I have-we are well advised to permit the promotion and use of lotteries for the purpose of raising money for possibly very justifiable and good causes.
Let me draw attention to the promoters and advertisers of the western Canadian lottery who use the slogan "It's my turn". They have clever ads in the hope that you will participate in the lottery. I should like to point out that in this country there are a fair number of provisions in the law to protect the public from misleading advertising and I am wondering if the western Canadian lottery advertisements are not, in fact, bordering on misleading advertising in using that slogan; because if you look at their various ads you come away with the impression that one of the people in the ad is going to win the next lottery, which is not the case at all. They might, but you do not even know if they have a ticket.
The real point-and I would like to present this very seriously to the minister-is whether we are not encouraging, through the provisions in Bill C-71, participation in lotteries which may be for a good cause but the advertisements for which might create false hopes. I wonder whether the bill does not encourage betting on a large scale, and whether it is not just another move to promote more

widespread betting facilities, off-track betting facilities, for example. We know that lottery tickets are being bought by people living at the poverty level who hope to improve their lot. So I would like to present my concern to the minister and say to him that I seriously question whether the legalization of interprovincial lotteries, although they enjoy wide participation by Canadians, is really in the best interests of the Canadian public at present.
The second point I should like to make relates to the provisions regarding breathalyzer tests and alcohol-related crimes. I believe that driving an automobile is a privilege in our society and that it carries certain responsibilities. Many of us have been concerned when another person has been involved in an accident and it is proved that the person involved in the accident was impaired. But often the attitude seems to be that the person was not entirely responsible. There is a feeling in society that a person who is impaired and involved in an accident often gets off easier than the person who is not impaired and gets involved in an accident.
I commend the minister for the provisions he brings in, especially in view of the fact that youth is turning more and more to alcoholic beverages. I shall refer to a study made by Dr. Morris Chafetz, director of the national institute of alcohol abuse and alcoholism in the United States. He points out that in the United States alone, by the tenth grade 50 per cent of the nation's youth report that they are drinking at night in cars. I am sure the minister has other statistics with regard to murders, assaults, rape and other sexual crimes wherein the use of alcohol is an important factor in their commission.
In our society we all feel that we want to be happy and good looking and to remain forever young and have hair on our head. For example, what do we see in the alcohol ads on television? The liquor ads we see show young people who are good looking and having fun together with friends. This is the type of promotion we use. We do not show what happens when there is alcohol abuse. I should like to encourage the minister to enforce our legislation, whereby those who are convicted of impaired driving are taken off the road and their licences lifted for a period of time. I do not believe fines are effective, at least not in our society today. It is one of the risks people have to take.
I said that I would be brief. I commend the minister for taking at least what I feel to be very positive steps. Through a public education system as well as enforcible laws we can show society that alcohol abuse is not to be tolerated and that the carnage on our highways, loss of property, loss of life and loss of family relationships are prices society simply does not want to pay. Rather, we should direct our attention to prevention, and where there is the commission of a crime under the provisions, the law should be very swift and very sure. I commend the minister for this bill.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE, CROWN LIABILITY ACT, IMMIGRATION ACT, PAROLE ACT JURISDICTION GIVEN TO CANADIAN COURTS TO TRY PERSONS FOR CERTAIN OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext:
In order not to detain members, may I quickly acknowledge very sincerely the kind remarks that many have made on my appointment as Minister of Justice. It is a somewhat awe inspiring position when one considers the predecessors from both sides that have occupied the office in Canada. I say awe inspiring, and somewhat intimidating, knowing the very eminent counsel that occupy places in this House and also those in the House who, while not lawyers, have a very deep and informed interest in matters relating to our criminal law. I truly appreciate the comments and can assure hon. members that I have always tried to conduct myself with an open mind with regard to suggestions on policy coming from all corners of the House, and I shall continue to do so.
We have had a very thoughtful discussion on this bill and other matters relating to the criminal law and the administration of criminal justice in Canada. I am not able to deal with many of the points raised in the five minutes left to me. All I can do is deal with the very useful points that have been made on such questions as rape, bail, drinking offences, conditional discharges, comments about gun control, and other things, when the bill is in committee, which presumably will be next week.
Because the debate did range a little-and I think that was useful-I want to put the bill in perspective and make it clear that this is one of the series of Criminal Code amendments that this House has now become used to. We are putting through the House, almost yearly, amendments to the Criminal Code of a substantial, procedural and evidentiary nature in an attempt, in a very complex society, to keep the Criminal Code up to date in substance and direction. Bill 71 is one of the series of Criminal Code amendment bills offered in an attempt to keep the law up to date.
Many members touched upon a point with which I agree completely-that simply amending the law from time to time or annually adjusting the Criminal Code is not solely
Criminal Code
the way to deal with the criminal law and criminal justice system. This is an important bill which makes important changes to the law substantially and procedurally but, as hon. members have pointed out, there are many other things that have to be done and need to be done.
I want to assure hon. members that the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) and I will be introducing a further series of amendments to the Criminal Code which are more comprehensive than Bill C-71 and will contain very important measures relating to law enforcement, prevention and detection of crime, changes in the parole system, release of prisoners and many other matters of importance. Some members pointed out that we have to go further than simply amending the law; we have to be concerned about the administration of justice. I agree with that.
At the attorneys general meeting held in Halifax on October 23 and 24, I suggested to the attorneys general and got their consent and approval to the appointment of a committee to examine things such as the prosecutorial responsibility of government. This committee is now at work determining which level of government should be prosecuting which crimes, with the objective of determining which is the most effective rationale and effective distribution of prosecutorial responsibility in this country. I just want to read this into the record:
That the committee be further instructed to report upon the feasibility of specific actions that might be taken, in the form of administrative and other arrangements, for the more efficient utilization of available court facilities and prosecutorial personnel by both provincial and federal authorities in areas of prosecutorial responsibility that are of concern to both authorities.
That is a beginning in the way of dealing with the question that the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) raised about the delay in the administration of justice. The object of that committee's work and my work is to ensure that where there are criminals and criminal activity, the matter is investigated, put before a prosecutor, put before a magistrate or judge and dealt with as quickly as possible.
Across this country there are very long case loads. There are long delays between an investigation and a conviction. That is bad for the administration of the criminal law. It is demoralizing to the police officer who, often at considerable danger to himself, especially one working as an undercover agent on a narcotics offence, often at great expense to the taxpayer, and after a long and most thorough investigation, to have to wait six or nine months or maybe a year and a half before the case comes to trial and there is a conviction. That is bad for the morale of the police of this country. It is bad in terms of the criminal community. They think they can take advantage of this system of delays that are occurring in the administration of justice. They feel that because the law takes so long to work, they have a certain immunity. It is also bad from the point of view of the community which asks, I think legitimately, whether in fact the laws of this country are being enforced. Those are three things to which we should address ourselves.
Other members touched upon the Law Reform Commission and its work. I simply want to put it in the context of this bill. The Law Reform Commission has done, and is doing, an immense amount of work in the area of criminal law reform. Over the next three of four years we are going


Criminal Code
to see in this House and in this country a great number of measures to implement some of the proposals of the Law Reform Commission.
The Law Reform Commission has issued working papers on the meaning of guilt, principles of sentencing and disposition, discovery, restitution and compensation, fines, diversion, limits of the criminal law, obscenity, imprisonment and release, the criminal process and mental disorder. Some time in the near future we will have other working papers. At the beginning of the year we will have final reports from the commission on a code of criminal evidence, sentencing, pre-trial procedure, mental disorder and change in the substantive criminal law.
I am concerned, as are other members, that this work of the Law Reform Commission and the money, knowledge and opportunity that has gone into it do not just sit on a shelf somewhere. Already within the department I am gearing up people to take those reports, analyse them and make recommendations. I have persuaded the provincial attorneys general to appoint, with me, a co-ordinator so that there is co-ordination between the federal government and the ten provincial governments with regard to the work of the Law Reform Commission and the implementation of their reports. However, as has been emphasized by
many members, law reform is not solely a question of changing the law in this House or some provincial House.
As the commission has pointed out, and as many members have pointed out, we must change our attitudes, our procedures, our whole technique involving the administration of justice in this country. The work of the Law Reform Commission is important and it is for that reason I recently appointed Mr. Justice Lemaire, who has been vice-chairman of the commission, as chairman upon retirement of the present chairman. Thus, not only will the commission continue to have the advantage of Mr. Lemaire's capabilities but there will be continuity in the work the commission has been doing. I want to tie Bill C-71 into the further amendments which will be brought in through the Criminal Code and with the work of the Law Reform Commission which is very much before me and before the officials in my department.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
